# Sirach 47 — Disagreement Log

**Chapter:** Sirach 47 | **Date:** 2026-03-17 | **Total Disagreements:** 18

---

## Disagreement 1 — 47:2, "separated from" vs. "set apart from"

**EMET:** "David was separated from the children of Israel"
**LOGOS:** "David was set apart from the children of Israel"
**PNEUMA:** "David was chosen out from among the children of Israel"
**Issue:** Greek aphōristhē = was separated/set apart. The fat analogy implies David was the choicest portion. "Set apart" (LOGOS) has both a separation and a consecration sense; "separated" (EMET) is more literal; "chosen out" (PNEUMA) is interpretive.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "set apart" — it best captures the dual sense of both selection and consecration.

---

## Disagreement 2 — 47:3, "young goats" vs. "kittens"

**EMET:** "He played with lions as with young goats"
**LOGOS:** "He played with lions as with young goats"
**PNEUMA:** "He played with lions as if they were kittens"
**Issue:** Greek eriphoi = young goats/kids. EMET/LOGOS agree literally. PNEUMA domesticates "kittens" without Greek support.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA follows EMET/LOGOS: "young goats."

---

## Disagreement 3 — 47:4, "strike down the boasting of Goliath" vs. "bring down Goliath's bragging"

**EMET:** "struck down the boasting of Goliath"
**LOGOS:** "brought down the boastfulness of Goliath"
**PNEUMA:** "brought Goliath's bragging to a permanent end"
**Issue:** Greek alazoneian = boastfulness, arrogance. "Boasting" (EMET) is more concrete; "boastfulness" (LOGOS) is the abstract noun; PNEUMA adds "permanent" without support.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "brought down the boasting of Goliath."

---

## Disagreement 4 — 47:6, "daughters" vs. "women" of Israel

**EMET:** "the daughters of Israel mourned for him and praised him"
**LOGOS:** "the women of Israel acclaimed him for his ten thousands"
**PNEUMA:** "the women of Israel sang his praises — tens of thousands for David!"
**Issue:** Greek thugateres = daughters. The allusion is to 1 Sam. 18:6 where the women (thugateres) of Israel sang. EMET "daughters" is literal but "women" is more natural in English.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "women of Israel" but notes the literal "daughters" in the Greek.

---

## Disagreement 5 — 47:6, "mourned for him" vs. "acclaimed him" vs. "sang his praises"

**EMET:** "mourned for him and praised him"
**LOGOS:** "acclaimed him for his ten thousands"
**PNEUMA:** "sang his praises"
**Issue:** Greek apedexanto = received, welcomed, acclaimed. EMET "mourned" appears to read a different text — the Greek has them rejoicing, not mourning. LOGOS/PNEUMA are correct.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "acclaimed him for his tens of thousands and sang his praises."

---

## Disagreement 6 — 47:7, "made sport of many" vs. "made short work of many"

**EMET:** "his hand made sport of many"
**LOGOS:** "his hand made short work of many"
**PNEUMA:** "his hand dealt with many of them"
**Issue:** Greek enepaixen = mocked, made sport of. EMET "made sport of" is the more literal rendering; "made short work of" (LOGOS) is idiomatic but changes the nuance.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA retains "made sport of many" — the contemptuous dismissal of enemies is the point.

---

## Disagreement 7 — 47:8, "set his hands right" — what does this mean?

**EMET:** "he would set his hands right"
**LOGOS:** "he would set his hands aright"
**PNEUMA:** "he would set his hands in the right direction"
**Issue:** Greek kateuthunen tas cheiras = directed/set straight his hands. The gesture is uncertain — possibly lifting hands in prayer, or orienting oneself correctly before God. EMET/LOGOS agree; PNEUMA expands.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA follows EMET/LOGOS: "set his hands aright."

---

## Disagreement 8 — 47:9, "set singers before the altar" vs. "placed singers before the altar"

**EMET:** "He set singers before the altar"
**LOGOS:** "He placed singers before the altar"
**PNEUMA:** "He stationed singers before the altar"
**Issue:** Minor variation. Greek esthēsen = he set, placed. All convey the same.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "placed singers before the altar" (LOGOS).

---

## Disagreement 9 — 47:9, "sweet melody" — source

**EMET:** "from their sound he made sweet melody"
**LOGOS:** "with their voices made sweet melody"
**PNEUMA:** "their voices made the melody sweet"
**Issue:** Greek en tous upsalous autōn glukanan melos = by their songs they made melody sweet. LOGOS/PNEUMA agree on "voices." EMET "sound" is slightly more literal.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "from their voices he drew sweet melody" — preserving both David's role (he drew it) and the source (their voices).

---

## Disagreement 10 — 47:10, "beauty" vs. "splendor"

**EMET:** "He gave beauty to the feast days"
**LOGOS:** "He gave splendor to the festivals"
**PNEUMA:** "He added splendor to the festivals"
**Issue:** Greek euprepeia = comeliness, beauty, seemliness. "Beauty" (EMET) is more literal; "splendor" (LOGOS/PNEUMA) is more elevated.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "He gave beauty to the feast days" — "beauty" has the appropriate aesthetic sense.

---

## Disagreement 11 — 47:11, "took away his sins" vs. "forgave his sins"

**EMET:** "The Lord took away his sins"
**LOGOS:** "The Lord forgave his sins"
**PNEUMA:** "The Lord forgave his sins"
**Issue:** Greek apheilato = took away, removed. "Took away" (EMET) is more literal and perhaps more theologically precise — sins were actively removed rather than merely overlooked.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA retains "took away his sins" — the active removal imagery is stronger and more literal.

---

## Disagreement 12 — 47:11, "covenant of kings" vs. "royal covenant"

**EMET:** "a covenant of kings"
**LOGOS:** "a royal covenant"
**PNEUMA:** "a royal covenant"
**Issue:** Greek diathēkē basileōn = covenant of kings. "Covenant of kings" (EMET) could mean a covenant belonging to kings (possessive) or a covenant establishing kings. LOGOS/PNEUMA "royal covenant" is clearer.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "covenant of kings" — the unusual genitive form is intentional.

---

## Disagreement 13 — 47:14, "dark parables" vs. "riddling parables" vs. "proverbs full of hidden meaning"

**EMET:** "you filled it with dark parables"
**LOGOS:** "you filled it with riddling parables"
**PNEUMA:** "you filled it with proverbs full of hidden meaning"
**Issue:** Greek en ainigmasin = in riddles/enigmas. "Dark parables" (EMET) captures the obscurity; "riddling parables" (LOGOS) is more precise; PNEUMA over-expands.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "dark parables" — "dark" preserves the enigmatic quality of ainigma.

---

## Disagreement 14 — 47:19, the sexual sin verse

**EMET:** "you put your loins beside women"
**LOGOS:** "you laid yourself open to women"
**PNEUMA:** "you gave yourself to women"
**Issue:** Greek edōkas en gynaixin = you gave yourself to women. EMET's "loins beside women" is more literal and more explicit. LOGOS "laid yourself open" is a polite idiom; PNEUMA "gave yourself" is neutral.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "you laid yourself open to women" — honest without being graphic, and true to the Greek sense of vulnerability/yielding.

---

## Disagreement 15 — 47:20, "profaned your offspring" vs. "profaned your lineage"

**EMET:** "profaned your offspring"
**LOGOS:** "profaned your lineage"
**PNEUMA:** "shamed your descendants"
**Issue:** Greek ebebēlōsas to sperma sou = you profaned your seed. "Profaned" (EMET/LOGOS) is the correct word; "shamed" (PNEUMA) is weaker. "Offspring" (EMET) vs. "lineage" (LOGOS).
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "profaned your descendants" — combining "profaned" (stronger) with the plural "descendants."

---

## Disagreement 16 — 47:22, "root from himself" vs. "root from his own stock"

**EMET:** "a root from himself"
**LOGOS:** "a root out of his own stock"
**PNEUMA:** "a root from his own stock"
**Issue:** Greek riza ex autou = root from him. "From himself" (EMET) is most literal; "from his own stock" (LOGOS/PNEUMA) makes the family lineage explicit.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "a root from his own stock" — clearer for the genealogical point being made.

---

## Disagreement 17 — 47:23, "broad in folly" vs. "foolish in counsel"

**EMET:** "Rehoboam, broad in folly and lacking in sense"
**LOGOS:** "Rehoboam, foolish in counsel and lacking in sense"
**PNEUMA:** "Rehoboam, an empty-headed fool"
**Issue:** Greek Roboam platei boulen = Rehoboam of broad counsel (ironic: counsel that spread destruction). "Broad in folly" (EMET) captures the irony; "foolish in counsel" (LOGOS) interprets; PNEUMA reduces to insult.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA retains "broad in folly and lacking in sense" — the ironic force of "broad" is important.

---

## Disagreement 18 — 47:25, "vengeance came upon them" vs. "the day of reckoning arrived"

**EMET:** "until vengeance came upon them"
**LOGOS:** "until vengeance caught up with them"
**PNEUMA:** "until the day of reckoning arrived"
**Issue:** Greek ekdikēsis = vengeance, punishment. All convey the same; PNEUMA's "day of reckoning" is interpretive expansion.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "until vengeance came upon them" (EMET) — simple and direct.

---

*Total disagreements logged: 18*
